PS! U PERSONALITY OF THE MONTH
Owen J. Roberts, Tau '95
By Robert T. McChacken, Tau '04
A
LAWYER who reached the highest
rung of the profession�the Supreme
Court of the United States�served his
country on that august tribunal for fifteen
years, retired at the age of seventy to
devote his remaining years to the manage
ment of his farm and the study and discus
sion of the problem of international peace.
Brother Roberts recently accepted the of
fice of Dean of the University of Pennsyl
vania Law School, and has thrown himself
into the administration of that venerable
and outstanding institution with all of his
old vigor.
A graduate of the College in 1895 and
of the Law School of Pennsylvania in
1898, Brother Roberts began the practice
of law in the traditional Philadelphia man
ner
by hanging out his shingle and waiting
for the practice to come.
Legal partner
ships were few in the Philadelphia of the
nineteenth century. The tradition of the
Enghsh Bar still held. John G. Johnson
dominated the scene� and John G. John
son had no
partners. So Brother Roberts
started on his own, supplementing his in
come
by lecturing in the Law School from
which he had received his degree.
Very soon, however, his vigorous per
sonality, keen intellect and tireless energy
attracted the attention of older lawyers and
pubhc officials. He was
appointed Assistant
District Attorney�an
appointment that
came to him wholly without political in
fluence, but solely because of the admira
tion of the man and some of his work by
the then newly elected District Attorney.
He quickly became the wheel horse of
that office, tryuig many of the most diffi
cult cases and preparing briefs for the
Chief when novel and unsettled points
were
presented for argument. A term of
service in the District Attorney's office has
launched many young men on careers of
distinction, and Roberts was no
exception.
Trial work in civil cases
began to come to
him in increasing volume. He was retained
in the widest variety of cases, by clients
ranging from the humblest workman to
banks, railroads and large corporations. His
success, before both juries and appellate
courts, was
phenomenal. Tall, of com
manding presence, with a fine voice, a
lightning-like grasp of the unexpected sit
uation, turning it to his instant advantage,
above all a manner which carried with it
a conviction of sincerity and absolute be
lief in the cause of his cHent, he was at
all times during a trial or
argument the
centre of attraction in the court room. As
the recognition of these qualities became
wide-spread, he was retained so
frequently
as senior counsel at the suggestion of other
lawyers, that, by the time he left the Bar
for the Bench, the bulk of his practice
emanated from this source.
In 1912 he formed a
partnership with
two of his friends, Wilham W. Mont
gomery, Jr. and Charles L. McKeehan, an
intimate association which continued until
the appointment of Mr. McKeehan to the
United States District Court for the East
ern District of Pennsylvania in 1923, and
thereafter, as Roberts and Montgomery,
until President Hoover elevated him to the
Supreme Court in 1930.
Undoubtedly the most widely knovra
piece of litigation in which he participated
was the trial, as Government Counsel, in
association with former Senator Pomerene
of Ohio, of the cases
arising out of the oil
scandals of the Harding administration.
Appointed by President Coolidge to this
difficult assignment, he conducted the
trials, both civil and criminal with such
consummate skill that all of the oil lands
were recovered by the Government and
the principal pubhc official involved in
the conspiracy. Secretary of the Interior
Albert B. Fall, was convicted and sent to
jad. It was this litigation which made
Brother Roberts a national figure and ren34

dered his selection to fill a
vacancy on the
Supreme Court a natural and anticipated
event.
There followed fifteen years of service
of the most arduous and exacting kind, on
that, the most powerful Court in the
world, first as the youngest of the "nine
old men" presided over
by Chief Justice
Hughes, and latterly as the last but oneChief Justice Stone�of that celebrated
group. His term of service covered two of
the most difficult periods in American his
tory�the entire span of the great depres
sion and the whole of World War II. A
dominant personality in the White House,
a
sharply novel political, social and eco
nomic philosophy permeating the thought
of the country, legislation emerging from
the halls of Congress and of the Assem
blies of many States radically in advance
of previous constitutional concepts, pre
sented to the Court a series of complex
and perplexing problems, many of which
had to be met and determined without
benefit of any precedent whatever. It is
too early to assess the contribution of
Brother Roberts to the record of the Court
as
history will ultimately appraise it. Yet
it can be stated, and will be remembered
by many, that when he submitted his resig
nation to President Truman in June, 1945,
the news was greeted in many parts of the
nation with regret amounting almost to
dismay. Despite the utmost divergence of
opinion, he had earned and retained the
complete confidence of the country.
In December, 1941, immediately after
the attack on Pearl Harbor, he was
ap
pointed by President Roosevelt head of a
commission which visited the scene and
reported upon the circumstances of the
raid. This report, the first on the subject,
has been subjected to the most rigid Con
gressional scrutiny, and has emerged as
authoritative in every detail.
In the autumn of 1945, he rejoined his
former partners in Philadelphia, not as a
member of the firm, but in a
happy asso
ciation which left him free to accept such
employment, legal or other, as came to his
hand. A firm believer in a Federation of
the Western Democracies as the only solu
tion of the problem of world peace, he has
travelled thousands of miles and delivered
countless addresses on this subject. Equal
ly convinced that universal military serv
ice is at least a
temporary necessity in the
atomic age, he has been one of the lead
ers in that movement and has appeared
before Congressional committees and Cab
inet officers on numerous occasions in its
behalf. Most recently, when a sudden and
unexpected vacancy occurred in the office
of Dean of the University of Pennsylvania
Law School, from which he had graduated
and in which he had been a
professor of
law for a number of years, he yielded to
the urging of the Trustees and accepted
the post of Dean of the School. Though
his administration has just begun, there
are
already signs that it will be one of the
happiest and most distinguished, from the
standpoints of both faculty and students,
in the history of the institution. The very
atmosphere of the place is electric with
the enthusiasm which he inspires.
In 1904 he married the lovely Elizabeth
Rogers, of Fairfield, Connecticut, and they
have one daughter, Mrs. Charles Hamilton,
and two grandchildren, Owen Roberts and
Deborah Hamilton. He and Mrs. Roberts
reside on his seven hundred acre farm near
Phoenixville, in Chester County, Pennsyl
vania, where he maintains a herd of well
over a hundred registered Guernseys pro
ducing grade A milk in paying quantities.
He is an enthusiastic Psi U, and not a few
of the brothers are
frequent visitors at his
farm. This little article is written by one
of them.

1949 CONVENTION TO BE HELD WITH
THE ZETA CHAPTER
Home of the Zeta
THE
1949 Annual Convention of the Psi Upsilon Fraternity wiH be held on Monday,
Tuesday and Wednesday, June 20, 21 and 22, under the auspices of the Zeta Chapter,
at Hanover, New Hampshire. This will be the 107th Convention of Psi Upsilon, held in
the 116th year of the Fraternity.
The Zeta Chapter is 107 years old, having been founded on May 10, 1842, seventy-two
years after the founding of Dartmouth College. It was the first chapter of any social
Greek letter Fraternity to make its home on the Dartmouth campus, although the fourth
chapter of Phi Beta Kappa had been, established there in 1787. The Zeta Chapter House,
shown above, was built in 1908 and remodeled in 1940.

DIAMOND CLUB BECOMES EPSILON OMEGA
OF PSI UPSILON
ON Saturday, February 26, 1949, at the
University Club of Chicago, Psi Up
silon added Epsilon Omega, Northwestern
University, to its list of 28 active chapters.
The formal installation of the new
chapter,
and the initiation of 27 new members, was
held during the afternoon and was fol
lowed by a formal banquet that evening.
The inaugural week-end wound up with
an
open house at
Epsilon Omega's new
home in Evanston, Illinois, on
Sunday
afternoon.

the Epsilon Omega, was elected President
at the first formal rneeting, and Byron W.
Kinney, '49, John D. Kenner, '50, and
John J. Zebell, '49, were elected VicePresident, Secretaty, and Treasurer, re
spectively.

The Origin of Epsilon Omega
Epsilon Omega began as The Diamond
Club of Northwestern University. Original
ly it .consisted of ten undergraduate mem
bers headed by Brother Kent who had
been initiated into Xi in 1945 and had
transferred to Northwestern after the war
to finish college. Diamond was
formally
recognized as a local fraternity by the In
terfraternity Council of Northwestern in
October, 1947. Following its recognition,
the chapter-to-be subsisted in a
meeting
room in the Student Union, borrowed from
the University, and a "home" in a
quonset
hut on the campus.
Meetings,- conversations, and an inter
change of letters with Psi U alumni of the
Chicago area resulted, at the Founders'
Day Banquet in 1947, in the appointment
of a
steering committee by the Executive
Council of Psi U alumni in Chicago to in
vestigate and, if thought desirable, support
Diamond's petition for membership in
the national fraternity. Dan H. Brown,
Omega '16, and his thirteen other commit

"Brandy" Died Today
1939-1949
The following touching letter was sent to
The Diamond by our faithful contributor and
Archivist, Henry C. Trundle, Xi '21. Brother
Trundle explains that "Brandy" was a
gorgeous St. Bernard dog, guardian of the Xi
and a
campus favorite, until Brother "Red"
Travis took him to his home at Weston, Mass.,
where he lived, as it were, at pasture.
March 14, 1949
Dear Brothers:
This is the day we all selfishly have
dreaded, when faithful, loveable "Brandy,"
mascot-emeritus of the Xi, went to sleep. He
has joined his master and our brother, "Bill"
Evans (Xi '40, killed in the war) in their
eternal home. If you had seen him lose so
much weight and strength these past few
weeks as the ravages of Bright's disease
finally took its toll, you would be glad for
him that he is at peace. By hand-feeding and
every other possible and kindly way, Mrs.
Travis had kept him fairly well until this past
weekend. Then when he could not rise with
out assistance, we had to decide that it would
be mercfful to have him put to sleep. It was
a terrible decision for us to make, for we loved
him hke a brother.
So "Brandy" sleeps between two pines on
the top of our wooded hill, and every time
we look out there to the sunset we'll think of
how much he meant to us and to thousands of
Xi and Wesleyan men� of how he exemplified
in so
many ways all that's best in the spirit of
Wesleyan and our Psi U brotherhood. His por
trait, hanging in the Xi, is a
symbol of his
friendship warm and true.
To have had him as a member of our
family these past two years was a rich and
joyous experience. We'll revere his memory
"until the sands of time are run."
Yours in the bonds.
The family of Harold G. Travis, Xi '20

of Northwestern, petitioner of Psi Upsfion

year, was initiated as the
Epsilon Omega. A brief history of the Dia
mond Club is as follows:
Diamond was
formally recognized as a local
fraternity by the Interfraternity Council of
Northwestern, October 21, 1947. Prior to this
time the Diamond Club was
organized by a
group of ten undergraduates, headed by Dick
Kent of the Xi. Early in September several
members of the Diamond Club visited the
Omega chapter at the University of Chicago,
where they received much encouragement and
helpful advice. A 'fist of several alumni ac
tives in the Psi U club of Chicago was ob
tained at the Omega and many of these men
were contacted, Mr. Dan H. Brown in par
ticular, and a
meeting was planned between
the Diamond Club and Psi Us living in this
area. Several more of these meetings followed,
each time with more alumni meeting the
group. At a Psi U Club of Chicago Executive
Council meeting a resolution was
passed to
the effect that: (1) the idea, of a
chapter at
Northwestern would be supported, and (2) the
Diamond Club would be supported and given
all possible help toward becoming a
chapter
of Psi Upsfion at Evanston. This resolution
was
unanimously passed at the Founders' Day
dinner of the Chicago Psi U Club.
In order to insure the maintenance of the
high standards of Psi Upsilon, all rushing
activities were
supervised by Psi U alumni
and actives from the various chapters living
in the Chicago area.
Following this policy of
careful selection. Diamond continued a
policy
of restricted membership.

U Club of Chicago, including the foUowing
alumni, helped the Diamond Club immeas
urably: Dan H. Brown, Chairman, Omega
'16; B. Bourke Corcoran, Omega '15; MiUer
Cross, Psi '10; Harold Anderson, Xi '12; Frank
Guthrie, Tau '24; A. J. Irvin, Zeta '02; W. B.
Presba, Sigma '32; B. E. Nevraian, Omega '17;

Meyers, Omicron '21; Henry W. Smith,
Omega '23; E. B. Pierce, Beta '13.
The new
Epsilon Omega now looks forward
to the coming years during which it hopes
to continue the spirit and good fellowship of
Psi Upsfion.
